name: The Apology
blurb: Five years late, one sibling comes to say sorry, and the other has kept a secret too
title: The Apology: 2-Person Drama Script for Siblings
description: A 4-minute drama duet for 2 actors playing adult siblings: an apology five years late meets a confession nobody expected. Free to perform and film.
h1: The Apology: a 4-Minute Drama Script for 2 Siblings
logline: Morgan missed their mother's last weeks and arrived the day after the funeral. Five years later, Morgan turns up at Casey's door with a speech and a tin of biscuits, but Casey has been rehearsing something too.
setting: The kitchen of Casey's flat, a weekday evening. Props: a biscuit tin, two mugs, a kettle, an old envelope.

roles.name: Morgan
roles.note: 30 to 45, any gender. The older sibling who moved away. Has come to apologise and wants to be forgiven tonight.

roles.name: Casey
roles.note: 28 to 42, any gender. The younger sibling who stayed and nursed their mother. Wants the apology, and dreads what comes after it.

script.action: CASEY fills the kettle. MORGAN stands by the door, still in a coat, holding a biscuit tin.

script.say: I brought these. The ginger ones. Mum's recipe. I tried, anyway.
You bake now?
I burn now. These are the survivors.

script.action: Casey almost smiles. Puts the tin on the table without opening it.

script.say: You can sit down. You don't need permission.
I wasn't sure.
Five years and you weren't sure if you could sit in a chair.
I wasn't sure about any of it. I wrote it down. What I wanted to say. I've got it on my phone.
Of course you have.
Can I just say it? Before you're kind to me, or before you're not?

script.action: Casey leans on the counter. Nods.

script.say: I should have come home when she got sick. I told myself the job needed me. I told myself you had it handled. You always had it handled. And I came back the day after the funeral, with a suitcase, like I was visiting.
You brought flowers.
I brought flowers to an empty house. I'm sorry, Casey. I'm sorry you did it alone. I'm sorry I made you be the strong one, because I was scared of being the useless one.

script.action: The kettle clicks off. Neither moves.

script.say: Is that the end?
There was more. It was mostly the word sorry.
Okay.
Okay?
I mean, thank you. I mean, I waited five years for that, and now I don't know where to put it.
You don't have to put it anywhere. I'm not asking you to say it's fine.
Good. Because it isn't.
I know.
Do you? You sent a card every New Year. With a photo of your balcony.
I didn't know what else to send.
Your face. You could have sent your face.
I'm sending it now. Late. It's a bit older.

script.action: Casey makes the tea, slowly, back turned to Morgan.

script.say: Do you know what the worst part was? Not the hospital. Not the nights. It was that she kept asking for you. Every day. Is Morgan coming? Has Morgan called?
I know. I'm sorry.
No. You don't know.

script.action: Casey turns around. Puts both mugs down. Keeps hold of one.

script.say: The last week. The doctor said days, not weeks. And Mum said, call Morgan. Tell Morgan to come now.
You told me it was stable. You texted me. Stable, don't worry.
I know what I texted you.
Casey.

I'd been there every single day for eight months. Every day. And you were going to fly in for the last three and be the one she cried over. I couldn't. I wanted her to myself. Just once, I wanted to be the one she was waiting for.

script.action: Silence. Morgan stands up. Sits down again.

script.say: So all this time.
All this time I've let you think it was only your fault. Because it was easier than saying that.
I'd have come. If you'd said.
I know. That's why I didn't say.
I hated you, just then. For about one second.
Only one?
I've spent five years hating myself. I'm out of practice with anyone else.

script.action: A long pause. Morgan opens the biscuit tin. Takes one. Pushes the tin across.

script.say: They're terrible. I put in twice the ginger.
She did that too. She said it was on purpose.
So. Two terrible children.
One terrible biscuit.

script.action: Casey takes an old envelope from a drawer. Sets it in front of Morgan. Morgan's name is on the front.

script.say: She wrote you this. The night before. I've had it five years.
What does it say?
I don't know. I never opened it. It wasn't mine to take as well.

script.action: Morgan holds the envelope. Doesn't open it. Reaches across the table instead and takes Casey's hand.

script.say: Read it with me.

script.action: Casey hesitates, then pulls a chair round to Morgan's side. Lights down as the envelope tears.

ul: A table and two chairs centre, a counter or side table upstage for the kettle. The table is the border between them for most of the scene.
Morgan stays in the coat until the first apology lands. Taking it off, or deciding not to, is a choice the actor can make in the moment.
Casey's confession is played leaning on the counter with a mug in hand, as if Casey needs something to hold on to.
The ending is a single move: Casey pulls a chair round to Morgan's side of the table. Leave the space between them empty until then so the move reads.
For a self-tape, frame both actors at the table in one wide shot, or tape each side in a single with a reader. For audio, the kettle, the tin lid and the envelope tearing do the staging for you.
Morgan's speech is memorised, not read. Morgan has said it in the car a hundred times; the danger is that it sounds rehearsed, so let one line break the pattern.
Casey's first beat is not anger but numbness. Casey has wanted this apology for years and it does not fix anything, which is more upsetting than rage.
The confession must come fast, in one breath, before Casey can talk themselves out of it. Then stop dead.
Morgan's key line is I'd have come. If you'd said. Play it without blame. The pain is that both of them are right.
The biscuit joke is a release valve. Let the audience laugh; it makes the envelope hit harder.
Common mistake: crying from the first line. Save the tears, or skip them. Restraint is more moving than sobbing.
Change the loss: a father's shop that closed, a grandparent's house that was sold, a family pet that died while one sibling was away. Keep the hidden message.
Play it as two childhood best friends instead of siblings; the one who moved away and the one who stayed.
End on the letter itself: have Morgan read the first line aloud, and write what the mother said as a part-two monologue.

prompts.keyframe: Small home kitchen in the evening, a kettle steaming on a counter, an adult in a coat standing by the doorway holding a biscuit tin, another adult at the counter with their back half turned, soft tungsten light, cinematic still, 16:9.
shots: Medium shot, static camera, an adult sits at a kitchen table speaking a careful apology while the sibling listens by the counter, quiet tense mood, warm evening light.
Slow push-in on an adult at a counter turning around with a mug, confessing quickly and emotionally, the other at the table goes still.
Close-up on hands sliding an old envelope across a kitchen table, then one hand reaching to hold the other's, gentle and bittersweet, soft light.

faq.q: Can we use The Apology in a drama competition or post it online?
faq.a: Yes. It is an original script under CC BY 4.0. Perform it, film it or record it anywhere, including monetised channels, and credit Script: cv.cm.

faq.q: Do the siblings have to be a brother and a sister?
faq.a: No. Both roles work for any gender, and the stage directions use only names, so any pairing of brothers, sisters or a mix plays without changes.

faq.q: How long is it and where are the big pauses?
faq.a: About 4 minutes. Allow three real pauses: after Morgan's apology, after Casey's confession, and before Morgan says Read it with me. Those silences are part of the running time.
